advantage_archetypes.name: The coached prodigy
advantage_archetypes.description: Identified early by an institutional pipeline, developed by dedicated coaches, and backed by a natural physical or talent edge. Common in sports and performance arts.

sample_trajectories.event: Earned a PhD from Harvard in mathematical logic at age 18 and published his first mathematical paper in the Messenger of Mathematics.
Studied under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge University and David Hilbert at the University of Göttingen, the two leading centers of mathematics in Europe.
Appointed as an instructor in mathematics at MIT, beginning a 45-year association with the institution.
Received the Bôcher Memorial Prize from the American Mathematical Society for his work in mathematical analysis.
Published Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine, founding the field of cybernetics.
Awarded the National Medal of Science for his contributions to mathematics, engineering, and biological sciences.
Died on March 18, 1964, in Stockholm, Sweden, while on a lecture tour.
Received MSc in Mathematics from Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
Discovered nondeterministic finite automata with Dana Scott during IBM Research summer program; completed PhD at Princeton.
Published seminal paper 'Finite Automata and Their Decision Problem' with Dana Scott in IBM Journal of Research and Development.
Won the ACM Turing Award with Dana Scott for their joint work on automata theory and nondeterministic machines.
Died on April 14 in Jerusalem.
Read Russell's Principia Mathematica in a Detroit library over three days and identified errors, leading to a correspondence with Bertrand Russell.
Ran away from home to the University of Chicago, began studying under Rudolf Carnap.
Co-authored 'A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity' with Warren McCulloch, proposing the first mathematical model of a neural network.
Moved to MIT with McCulloch; became a key figure in the cybernetics movement alongside Wiener and von Neumann.
Died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, from complications related to alcoholism and isolation.

advantage_archetypes.name: The multiply-advantaged
advantage_archetypes.description: High advantage scores across several dimensions. Multiple compounding early advantages.

sample_trajectories.event: Released the Morris worm from MIT, the first Internet worm, infecting approximately 10% of internet-connected computers
First person convicted under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act; sentenced to 3 years probation, 400 hours community service, and $10,050 fine
Co-founded Viaweb with Paul Graham, one of the first software-as-a-service companies
Viaweb acquired by Yahoo for approximately $49 million in stock, rebranded as Yahoo Store
Co-founded Y Combinator with Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, and Trevor Blackwell
Received tenure at MIT in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
Elected to the National Academy of Engineering
Founded Milo.com, a local product search engine indexing real-time store inventory, after dropping out of Wharton.
Sold Milo.com to eBay for approximately $75 million; became Head of Local at eBay.
Founded Atomic, a San Francisco-based startup studio and venture capital firm, with an initial $20 million fund.
Co-founded Hims & Hers Health, which became the second-fastest U.S. company to reach $1 billion valuation.
Atomic raised $260 million in additional funding; Hims & Hers went public via SPAC at a $1.6 billion valuation.
Obtained real estate license; interned for a local developer while attending University of Colorado Boulder.
Moved to New York City and joined Douglas Elliman; sold first property, an $8.2M penthouse at the Park Imperial.
Named to Forbes 30 Under 30 list for real estate.
Sold the most expensive home in Miami, a $47M estate in Indian Creek, celebrating his 25th birthday.
Co-brokered the biggest residential sale in US history: Ken Griffin's $238M penthouse at 220 Central Park South.
Co-founded Official Partners, a luxury real estate brokerage, with brother Tal.
Arrested in December 2024 on federal sex trafficking charges along with brothers Tal and Alon; held without bail.

advantage_archetypes.name: The elite-ecosystem founder
advantage_archetypes.description: Elite schooling, grew up in a frontier hub, and found exceptional cofounders/peers. The classic tech-founder advantage stack — place, pipeline, and people.

sample_trajectories.event: Became the first RFC Editor on April 7, 1969, a role he would hold for nearly 30 years, editing over 2400 RFCs defining Internet standards.
Completed PhD in Computer Science at UCLA under Dave Farber.
Joined USC's Information Sciences Institute, where he would spend the rest of his career directing IANA and editing RFCs.
Co-authored foundational RFCs for the Domain Name System (RFC 881, 882, 920), establishing the hierarchical naming system used by the Internet today.
Brokered the plan to create ICANN, transitioning Internet governance from US government to a nonprofit; died October 16 from complications after heart surgery.
Graduated from Cambridge with First Class Honours in mathematics and joined the Telecommunications Research Establishment to work on radar under Freddie Williams.
Co-developed the Williams-Kilburn tube for CRT storage at Manchester and published an influential internal report on binary digital storage in December 1947.
Co-designed and built the Manchester Baby, the world's first stored-program electronic digital computer, which ran its first program on 21 June 1948.
Led development of the Ferranti Mark 1, the world's first commercially available computer.
Led the development of the Atlas computer, one of the first time-sharing multiprocessing computers with paging and pipelining.
Became head of the Department of Computer Science at the University of Manchester.
Died on 17 January 2001 in Manchester after twenty years of quiet retirement.
Applied for his first patent on light modulating methods while at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at Penn.
Appointed chief engineer of the ENIAC project at the Moore School, collaborating with John Mauchly on the first general-purpose electronic digital computer.
ENIAC was completed and publicly dedicated on February 15, 1946 at the University of Pennsylvania, acclaimed as a major computing breakthrough.
Co-founded the Eckert-Mauchly Computer Corporation to build the UNIVAC, the first commercial computer in the United States.
UNIVAC I was delivered to the U.S. Census Bureau, becoming the first commercially produced computer in the United States.
Received the National Medal of Science for his contributions to computing.
Died on June 3, 1995 in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania.

advantage_archetypes.name: The mentored talent
advantage_archetypes.description: Strong mentorship and institutional pipeline, but modest family background. A mentor or coach opened doors that family wealth couldn't.

sample_trajectories.event: Selected through math olympiads for special physics-mathematics high school in Kiev.
Completed Master's degree at Moscow University under Andrey Kolmogorov.
Independently discovered NP-completeness (Cook-Levin theorem); completed Candidate degree at Moscow University.
Emigrated from Soviet Union to the United States and joined MIT as a researcher.
Earned PhD from MIT under Albert Meyer.
Joined Boston University as Professor of Computer Science.
Awarded the Knuth Prize for discovery of NP-completeness and development of average-case complexity.
Elected to the US National Academy of Sciences.
Received BS in Electrical Engineering from MIT.
Received MS in Electrical Engineering from MIT.
Earned PhD in Mathematics from MIT, introducing the Blum axioms for computational complexity in his thesis.
Joined UC Berkeley as tenured associate professor of electrical engineering and computer science.
Won the ACM Turing Award for contributions to computational complexity theory and its application to cryptography and program checking.
Joined Carnegie Mellon University as Bruce Nelson Professor of Computer Science.
Received BS in Mathematics from Caltech.
Co-authored first planarity testing tech report with Hopcroft at Stanford.
Completed PhD at Stanford with thesis 'An Efficient Planarity Algorithm' under Robert Floyd.
Published 'Efficient Planarity Testing' in Journal of the ACM, establishing the linear-time planarity algorithm.
Won the first Rolf Nevanlinna Prize for outstanding contributions to mathematical aspects of information sciences.
Joined Princeton University as James S. McDonnell Distinguished University Professor of Computer Science.
Won the ACM Turing Award with John Hopcroft for fundamental achievements in algorithm design and analysis.

advantage_archetypes.name: The pipeline-routed talent
advantage_archetypes.description: Modest family background, but accessed an institutional pipeline (sports system, academy, scholarship) and grew up in a field hub. Place and pipeline opened doors that family wealth couldn't.

sample_trajectories.event: Graduated from Tufts University with a degree in computer science; joined Claris, an Apple subsidiary, developing Macintosh software.
Co-founded Ink Development Corp (later eShop Inc.) on May 10, an early online shopping software company.
Launched AuctionWeb (later eBay) on Labor Day weekend as a side project on his personal website.
eShop acquired by Microsoft on June 11; quit his day job at General Magic to focus on eBay full-time.
eBay went public; Omidyar became a billionaire shortly after the IPO.
Founded Omidyar Network, a philanthropic investment firm.
Founded First Look Media, including The Intercept news organization.
Released Drupal 1.0.0 as open-source software on January 15, 2001, from his University of Antwerp dorm project.
Co-founded Acquia with Jay Batson to provide commercial support and services for Drupal.
Named to MIT Technology Review TR35 as one of the top 35 innovators under 35; also named Young Entrepreneurs of Tech by BusinessWeek.
Defended PhD dissertation in computer science at Ghent University on profiling and instrumentation of the JVM.
Acquia helped re-launch Whitehouse.gov on Drupal, cementing Drupal's enterprise credibility.
Acquia acquired by Vista Equity Partners in a deal valuing the company at approximately $1 billion.
Transitioned to Executive Chairman of Acquia as Chris Tranquill was appointed CEO.
Began writing a Pascal compiler for the Nascom microcomputer while studying at the Danish Technical University and co-founding PolyData, Copenhagen's first computer store.
Turbo Pascal 1.0 released by Borland, based on Hejlsberg's PolyPascal compiler; became one of the most commercially successful Pascal compilers ever.
Moved to California to become Chief Engineer at Borland as PolyData came under financial stress.
Led development of Borland Delphi as chief architect, combining Turbo Pascal's compilation speed with visual RAD for Windows.
Joined Microsoft as chief architect of Visual J++ and later designed C# for the .NET platform.
Designed and launched TypeScript to address JavaScript's lack of static typing; it became the top language used by 2025.
Leading the native port of TypeScript to Go (TypeScript 7) for a 10x performance improvement, with a release candidate available.

advantage_archetypes.name: The platform-native builder
advantage_archetypes.description: Grew up with online platforms and direct audience/customer exposure. Built things people used from an early age. Low traditional advantage, high digital-native leverage.

sample_trajectories.event: Moved to Sebastopol, California to work for O'Reilly Media; began blogging on EvHead.com and learning to code.
Co-founded Pyra Labs with Meg Hourihan on January 1; launched Blogger, one of the first blog-publishing platforms.
Pyra Labs and Blogger acquired by Google for an undisclosed sum.
Co-founded Twitter via Obvious Corporation with Jack Dorsey and Biz Stone.
Became CEO of Twitter, succeeding Jack Dorsey.
Founded Medium, an online publishing platform.
Co-founded Obvious Ventures, a venture capital firm focused on world-positive companies.
Stepped down from Twitter board of directors.
Co-created Phoenix (later Firefox) with Dave Hyatt; first public release Phoenix 0.1 on September 23, 2002.
Firefox 1.0 launched on November 9, 2004; downloaded 27 million+ times, challenging Internet Explorer's browser dominance.
Nominated for Wired magazine's Renegade of the Year award and included in Rolling Stone's 2005 hot list.
Co-founded Parakey, a web OS startup, with Joe Hewitt.
Parakey acquired by Facebook as its first acquisition; Ross joined Facebook as an engineer.
Left Facebook as Director of Product after six years to pursue new projects.
Purchased an $8.25 million condominium in Soho, New York City.
Began contributing to the Mozilla open-source project as a computer engineering student at the University of Auckland.
Hired as an intern at Netscape in Mountain View after his Mozilla contributions were noticed by engineer David Hyatt.
Led engineering for Firefox 1.0, the open-source browser that challenged Microsoft's Internet Explorer dominance.
Joined Google to lead user experience for the Chrome browser project.
Joined OpenAI to lead development of the Atlas browser, aiming to challenge Chrome.

advantage_archetypes.name: The hardship-forged athlete
advantage_archetypes.description: Physical talent plus early adversity that catalyzed drive, channeled through coaching. Common in combat sports and endurance events — hardship became fuel.

sample_trajectories.event: Won silver medal representing Poland at the International Mathematical Olympiad in Vietnam.
Co-authored 'Intriguing properties of neural networks' while at Google Brain, a foundational paper on adversarial examples in neural networks.
Co-founded OpenAI as one of its founding members alongside Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Ilya Sutskever.
Led OpenAI robotics team that created a robotic arm capable of solving a Rubik's Cube.
Continues as co-founder of OpenAI, leading work on GPT models, GitHub Copilot, and Codex.
Started Rude Boy Productions, a DJ company funded by bar mitzvah and babysitting savings, earning over $100K by high school graduation.
Graduated from Columbia University in under two years; hired as youngest analyst at McKinsey & Company.
Graduated from Columbia Business School with an MBA; joined Lazard in investment banking.
Selected as a White House Fellow, working for Secretary of the Treasury John W. Snow.
Became vice president at Goldman Sachs, serving as chief of staff for president and COO Gary Cohn.
Co-founded Compass, a real estate technology company.
Took Compass public on the New York Stock Exchange; company valued at approximately $6 billion.
Won the World Youth Chess Championship (Under-12) in Szeged with 8/9, ahead of future top players including Ponomariov and Grischuk.
Earned the title of chess grandmaster.
Won the Armenian Chess Championship and the World Junior Chess Championship in India.
Won the FIDE World Cup in Russia and entered the world's top 10 for the first time.
Led the Armenian team to Olympic gold medal, playing first board; also won the Chess960 World Championship.
Reached world No. 2 in the FIDE rankings with a rating of 2830, becoming the fourth-highest-rated player in history.
Switched federations from Armenia to the United States.

advantage_archetypes.name: The pipeline-routed talent
advantage_archetypes.description: Modest family background, but accessed an institutional pipeline (sports system, academy, scholarship) and grew up in a field hub. Place and pipeline opened doors that family wealth couldn't.

sample_trajectories.event: Joined Bell Labs as a Member of Technical Staff in the Computing Sciences Research Center, the lab that created Unix.
Wrote the first bitmap window system for Unix systems at Bell Labs.
Designed the Blit programmable bitmap graphics terminal with Bart Locanthi, later commercialized by AT&T as the DMD 5620.
Co-created UTF-8 character encoding with Ken Thompson, which became the dominant text encoding for the web.
Joined Google and began work on distributed systems infrastructure and the Sawzall programming language.
Co-created the Go programming language with Ken Thompson and Robert Griesemer, publicly released on November 10, 2009.
Retired from Google after nearly two decades, continuing personal projects such as the Ivy APL-like calculator.
Received BSc in mathematics from Tel Aviv University.
Received MSc in computer science from the Weizmann Institute of Science.
Completed PhD at Weizmann under Zohar Manna and co-invented the RSA public-key cryptosystem with Rivest and Adleman at MIT.
RSA paper published in Communications of the ACM, becoming one of the most cited papers in computer science history.
Returned to Israel to join the faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science at the Weizmann Institute.
Co-recipient of the ACM Turing Award with Rivest and Adleman for contributions to public-key cryptography.
Received the Israel Prize for computer science.
Received the Wolf Prize in Mathematics for fundamental contributions to mathematical cryptography.
Co-authored the seminal Goldwasser-Micali paper on probabilistic encryption at STOC, introducing semantic security to cryptography.
Completed PhD at UC Berkeley under Manuel Blum with thesis 'Probabilistic Encryption: Theory and Applications.'
Co-authored the foundational paper on zero-knowledge proofs with Micali and Rackoff.
Awarded the Godel Prize for work on interactive proofs.
Received the Grace Murray Hopper Award.
Won the ACM Turing Award jointly with Silvio Micali for foundational contributions to cryptography.
Became director of the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing at UC Berkeley, serving until 2024.

advantage_archetypes.name: The adversity-forged striver
advantage_archetypes.description: Early hardship acted as a catalyst. Low inherited advantage, but adversity created drive and resilience that compensated.

sample_trajectories.event: Co-founded Odeo, a podcasting company, with Evan Williams after his AudBlog startup merged with Williams' operation.
Co-founded Twitter within Odeo; coined the name 'Twitter' and helped design core features.
Ousted from Twitter by Evan Williams, who acquired Odeo's assets and renamed it Obvious Corporation.
Dropped out of University of Cincinnati and moved to San Francisco to work as a web developer at CNET on GameSpot and other sites.
Co-founded GitHub with Tom Preston-Werner and PJ Hyett; public launch in April 2008, reaching 100,000 users within a year.
GitHub raised Series A funding from Andreessen Horowitz at a valuation reportedly around $750 million.
Microsoft acquired GitHub for $7.5 billion in an all-stock deal; Wanstrath became a billionaire as the largest individual shareholder.
Founded Null Games, an independent game publishing studio, after leaving Microsoft.
Moved to San Francisco after graduating from North Central College; worked as a senior software engineer at CNET Networks.
Co-founded GitHub with Chris Wanstrath and Tom Preston-Werner; public launch in April 2008.
GitHub raised Series A from Andreessen Horowitz; company valued at approximately $750 million.
Microsoft acquired GitHub for $7.5 billion; Hyett's stake was estimated at close to $1 billion.
Founded AO Racing, a motorsport team competing in IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship.
Won the 24 Hours of Le Mans LMP2 Pro-Am class and led the IMSA LMP2 championship standings.

advantage_archetypes.name: The ordinary-background achiever
advantage_archetypes.description: Few documented early advantages. Achievement came from drive and timing rather than head start.

sample_trajectories.event: Released PHP 1.0 (Personal Home Page Tools) on June 8, 1995, via a Usenet newsgroup announcement.
Contributed to the Apache HTTP Server project and added the LIMIT clause to the mSQL DBMS.
Joined Yahoo! Inc. as an Infrastructure Architecture Engineer, helping migrate Yahoo to PHP-based tools.
Named to MIT Technology Review's list of top innovators for creating PHP, which by then powered over 12 million websites.
Joined Etsy as Distinguished Engineer, working on architecture, internationalization, payments, fraud, and security.
Wrote Gosling Emacs, the first Emacs implementation for Unix in C, while a PhD student at Carnegie Mellon University; it was later commercially distributed by UniPress Software.
Completed PhD in Computer Science at Carnegie Mellon University with thesis 'Algebraic Constraints' under Bob Sproull and Raj Reddy.
Led the original design and implementation of the Java programming language at Sun Microsystems, including its compiler and virtual machine.
Elected to the US National Academy of Engineering for the conception and development of Java and contributions to windowing systems.
Briefly joined Google, then became Chief Software Architect at Liquid Robotics, writing software for autonomous ocean-going robots.
Joined Amazon Web Services as Distinguished Engineer, working on IoT projects including AWS Greengrass.
Retired from Amazon Web Services in July 2024 after a career spanning nearly 50 years as a software engineer.
Devised Merkle's Puzzles, an early public-key cryptographic key exchange scheme, as an undergraduate at UC Berkeley.
Submitted the public-key cryptography paper to Communications of the ACM after encouragement from faculty member Bob Fabry.
Joined Diffie and Hellman at Stanford for the summer, becoming part of the public-key cryptography research team.
Completed PhD in Electrical Engineering at Stanford under Martin Hellman with thesis 'Secrecy, Authentication, and Public Key Systems.'
Joined Xerox PARC as a research scientist, where he designed the Khufu and Khafre block ciphers and the Snefru hash function.
Became Distinguished Professor of Computer Science at Georgia Tech before returning to California in 2006.
Received the IEEE Richard W. Hamming Medal jointly with Diffie and Hellman for work on public-key cryptography.

leverage_archetypes.name: The wave-riding specialist
leverage_archetypes.description: Rode a structural wave (tech platform, cultural shift) with deep, scarce expertise built through years of reps. Timing plus skill depth — the classic founder combo.

leverage_archetypes.name: The relentless practicer
leverage_archetypes.description: Thousands of hours of focused, concentrated practice. Got there through consistency and intensity — reps over timing.

leverage_archetypes.name: The opportunistic rider
leverage_archetypes.description: Caught a structural wave with enough reps to hang on. Timing was the primary lever — skill was adequate, not exceptional.

leverage_archetypes.name: The partnership lever
leverage_archetypes.description: A complementary team or partner was the primary leverage. Built something together that neither could alone.

leverage_archetypes.name: The early starter
leverage_archetypes.description: Started serious practice before 20 and accumulated significant reps. Consistency from an early age — the tortoise, not the hare.

leverage_archetypes.name: The network-native
leverage_archetypes.description: Embedded in a high-signal network that provided opportunities, feedback, and distribution. Network as the primary lever.

leverage_archetypes.name: The moderate lever
leverage_archetypes.description: Moderate leverage across several dimensions. Some reps, some timing, some network — but no dominant built advantage.

leverage_archetypes.name: The early-stage builder
leverage_archetypes.description: Low leverage scores across the board. The built advantages — reps, skill depth, timing, network — haven't compounded yet.
